titre: 146 Dead on a Saturday, a Commission of Inquiry Rather Than a Law
accroche: On March 25, 1911, a fire in a Manhattan workshop kills 146 people; the State of New York responds with an investigation, not a law passed in haste.
contenu_vulgarise:
On Saturday, March 25, 1911, at about 4:40 p.m., a fire breaks out on the eighth floor of the Asch Building, at the corner of Greene Street and Washington Place in Manhattan. The top three floors house the workshops of the Triangle Shirtwaist Company, where about 500 people work, the great majority of them young immigrant women sewing blouses. The fire starts in a bin of fabric scraps under a cutting table and spreads within minutes to the fabrics hanging all around. The door to the stairway on Washington Place is locked (a common practice to prevent theft and unauthorized breaks), the only outside fire escape collapses under the weight of the workers trying to flee, and the firefighters' ladders do not reach the burning floors. One hundred forty-six people die, 123 women and girls and 23 men; most from burns, asphyxiation, shock, or all three at once. Sixty-two jumped or fell from the windows.

## A Commission, Not a Law

The emotion is immediate, but it is not a law that follows first: it is a commission of inquiry. The State of New York creates the Factory Investigating Commission, chaired by State Senator Robert F. Wagner, with Al Smith, then majority leader of the Assembly, at his side. For several years, it has field investigators inspect factories across the state, hears 222 witnesses, and publishes its findings in several reports rather than a single text. These efforts produce 38 new labor laws in the State of New York; between 1911 and 1913 alone, 60 of the 64 laws it recommends are passed. New York thus becomes one of the most advanced states in the country on labor reform.

## The Shift

Two people connected with this inquiry carry it well beyond New York. Frances Perkins, a witness to the fire, becomes executive secretary of the New York City Committee on Safety and works with Wagner's investigating commission; Secretary of Labor from 1933 to 1945, she is the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet. Robert Wagner, who chaired the commission, later sits in the United States Senate, where he writes the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, which protects the right of private-sector employees to form unions and bargain collectively; the law is considered a founding text of American labor law.

The fire of March 25, 1911 therefore did not first produce a statute: it produced a method, investigate before legislating, and two careers that each, in their own way, left their mark on American labor law.

repere.texte: The fire of March 25, 1911 kills 146 people in the workshops of the Triangle Shirtwaist Company in New York. The commission of inquiry created afterward leads to 38 new labor laws in the state; between 1911 and 1913, 60 of the 64 laws it recommends are adopted.

carte.punch: 146 dead in a New York fire, and first an investigation before the laws.
carte.idee: On March 25, 1911, a fire kills 146 people in a Manhattan garment workshop, mostly women. The inquiry that follows is chaired by Robert Wagner, future author of the 1935 law on union rights, and puts Frances Perkins, future Secretary of Labor, to work.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The career of the first woman member of a U.S. presidential cabinet, from the 1911 fire to the New Deal.

quiz.question: Why does the Factory Investigating Commission, created after the 1911 fire, take several years to produce results rather than an immediate law?
choix: Because the governor of New York opposed any new safety rule
Because it visits factories, questions workers and employers, and has laws passed as its investigation proceeds rather than in a single text
Because the Triangle Shirtwaist Company delayed the inquiry with legal challenges
Because workplace safety was then solely a federal matter, and the federal government was slower to legislate
quiz.explication: The commission investigates in the field for several years and has its conclusions enacted as it goes, rather than answering the fire with a single text drafted in haste.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which factors made the toll of the March 25, 1911 fire in the Asch Building worse?
choix: The locked door, the collapsed fire escape, and firefighters' ladders that were too short
The complete absence of any emergency exit in the entire building
The firefighters' refusal to intervene before the arrival of the mayor of New York
A gas explosion that destroyed the first two floors of the building
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The door onto Washington Place is locked, the outside fire escape collapses under the weight of the workers, and the firefighters' ladders do not reach the burning floors.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Once a U.S. senator, what does Robert Wagner, who chaired the 1911 commission of inquiry, write?
choix: A federal law banning child labor in textile factories
The National Labor Relations Act of 1935, protecting the union rights of private-sector employees
The text creating federal labor inspection in every state
A law limiting women's working hours to eight hours a day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Robert Wagner, who chaired the commission after the fire, later writes as a senator the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, which protects the right of private-sector employees to form unions and bargain collectively.
